hints.title: Sketch one full period
hints.body: Locate the zeros and signs of sin(2x) over one period. Compare the two half-period areas by symmetry.
hints.recap: Replacing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> by a constant multiple changes the horizontal scale and hence the period of a trigonometric graph.
hints.pitfall: The sign of a function and its accumulated area are different quantities.
hints.pause: Draw one period and mark which signed areas cancel.

recall.reminder: Replacing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> by a constant multiple changes the horizontal scale and hence the period of a trigonometric graph.

hints.title: Track a partial period
hints.body: After removing complete periods, follow the accumulated signed area as the remaining endpoint moves through a period. Check negative endpoints and zero as well.
hints.recap: A definite integral is signed area; reversing its limits reverses its sign.
hints.pitfall: Cancellation over a whole period does not imply cancellation over every partial period.
hints.pause: Decide exactly where the running integral returns to zero, then test both logical directions.

recall.reminder: A definite integral is signed area; reversing its limits reverses its sign.

solution:
The graph of sin(2x) has period π. In one period it is positive for the first half and negative for the second; the two areas have equal magnitude.

Starting at any integer multiple of π, the running signed area first increases above 0 and then decreases back to 0 only at the end of that period. Thus it is positive at every point strictly inside a period and zero at its endpoints. Complete periods contribute 0; the same conclusion holds to the left of 0, with the orientation of an integral taken into account.

Therefore ∫0ksin(2x)dx=0 exactly when k is an integer multiple of π, including 0. R is both necessary and sufficient for S: answer A.
knowledgePattern: Use signed sine areas to prove both directions of a zero-integral condition
